hints.title: Write what a counterexample must do
hints.body: The premise is that n is prime. The conclusion is that n2+2 is not prime. A counterexample must make the premise true and the conclusion false.
hints.recap: Both n and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> must be prime to refute this implication.
hints.pitfall: An input outside the prime premise cannot disprove the conditional statement.
hints.pause: What two primality checks are needed for each listed n?

recall.reminder: A counterexample satisfies every hypothesis and violates the conclusion; for an implication, its premise must be true.

hints.title: Test the prime candidates
hints.body: Compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> separately for each candidate whose input is prime. Test the resulting integers for primality.
hints.recap: A true premise is only the first half of a counterexample check.
hints.pitfall: A result that is composite satisfies the stated conclusion rather than refuting it.
hints.pause: Record the premise and conclusion truth values for each candidate.

recall.reminder: A true premise is only the first half of a counterexample check.

hints.title: Apply the conditional test to every row
hints.body: Inspect your completed table and select only rows with a true premise and a false conclusion.
hints.recap: An input not meeting the prime hypothesis cannot refute the conditional.
hints.pitfall: Performing the calculation does not by itself make an input relevant.
hints.pause: Decide which listed candidates meet both counterexample requirements.

recall.reminder: An input not meeting the prime hypothesis cannot refute the conditional.

solution:
A counterexample needs n prime and n2+2 prime, because the stated conclusion says that the latter is not prime.

I: n=2 is prime, but 22+2=6 is not prime, so the claim holds in this case.

II: n=3 is prime and 32+2=11 is also prime. Thus the premise holds and the conclusion fails: this is a counterexample.

III: n=4 is not prime, so it does not satisfy the hypothesis and cannot refute the implication.

II only: C.
knowledgePattern: Counterexample requires a true antecedent and false conclusion
